title: Neurogenic pain
description: Facial and oral pain of neurogenic, vascular, or central origin — the differentials for the toothache that doesn't behave like a toothache.

problems.description: Lightning-shock pain on one side of the face triggered by touching a specific spot — shaving, eating, cold air — lasting only seconds.
problems.etiology: The most common neurological cause of facial pain. The thing is, nobody's quite sure what fires it — the current view is a sensory form of epilepsy, but some cases trace back to a vessel pressing on the nerve or to demyelination higher up [1]. So when a patient under 50 walks in with cranial-nerve neuralgia, you can't just call it idiopathic. Full neurological exam and MRI — these can be the presenting symptom of an intracranial tumour, skull-base metastases, HIV, syphilis, or MS [2].
problems.presentation: What you'll hear is an excruciating, paroxysmal electric-shock pain — rapid onset, seconds to under two minutes, one side of the face, in the trigeminal distribution [1]. There's always a trigger zone: a small patch of skin or mucosa where light touch, airflow, or chewing reliably fires it. Patients may stop shaving or washing the affected area entirely [1]. Strangely, it rarely wakes them at night [1]. Early on, there can be a prodromal phase where the pain doesn't yet fit the classic picture — and that's when the diagnostic errors happen, before the paroxysmal character declares itself [1].
problems.results: Here's the sequence that plays out far too often: the pain is mistaken for dental in origin, and patients end up with multiple extractions before anyone reaches the right diagnosis [1]. Diagnosis is by history alone — no objective signs, nothing to find on examination. Carbamazepine is both the treatment and the test: an 80% response rate means a good response to carbamazepine is itself diagnostic [1].
problems.definingCharacteristics: The defining feature that separates this from every other neuropain condition is the trigger zone: a small patch of facial skin or mucosa where light, innocuous contact (touch, airflow, chewing) reliably fires a paroxysmal electric-shock burst lasting only seconds [1]. No other condition in this origin has a discrete contact trigger zone.
problems.treatment: LA injection can break an acute pain cycle and doubles as a diagnostic test [1]. First-line drug: carbamazepine [1]. Also reach for gabapentin or pregabalin [1]. If drugs fail, surgical options range from peripheral (cryotherapy, alcohol/phenol nerve destruction, radiofrequency ablation) to central (microvascular decompression, glycerol or radiofrequency rhizotomy, gamma knife radiosurgery) [1].
problems.prognosis: Carbamazepine hits an 80% response rate and stays first-line [1]. A small proportion of cases turn out to reflect underlying demyelination or intracranial pathology — their prognosis is that of the underlying diagnosis, not of the neuralgia itself [2].

citations.quote: This is the most common neurological cause of facial pain, it is an excruciating condition affecting mainly the >50s, F > M. It presents as a paroxysmal shooting 'electric shock' type of pain of rapid onset and short duration (few seconds to less than 2min), affecting one side of the face in the distribution of the trigeminal nerve. It is often stimulated by touching a trigger point in the distribution of the trigeminal nerve. Patients may refuse to shave or wash the area which stimulates the pain although, strangely, they are rarely woken by it. In the early stages of the disease there may be a period of prodromal pain not conforming to the classical description and it may be difficult to arrive at a ∆; patients often have multiple extractions in an attempt to relieve the symptoms. It is thought to be a sensory form of epilepsy, although some cases are due to vascular pressure or nerve demyelination intracranially. ∆ is by the history, and carbamazepine is useful both therapeutically and diagnostically, with an 80% response rate. Injection of LA can break pain cycles and be useful diagnostically. Other useful drugs are gabapentin and pregabalin. Surgical management includes peripheral Rxs such as cryotherapy, chemical destruction of nerve (alcohol/phenol), or radiofrequency ablation and central neurosurgical procedures such as microvascular decompression, glycerol or radiofrequency rhizotomy, or gamma knife radiosurgery.

Patients under the age of 50yrs presenting with symptoms of cranial nerve neuralgia require full neurological examination and a MRI scan, as these may be the presenting symptoms of an intracranial neoplasm, skull base metastases, HIV, syphilis, or multiple sclerosis. Bilateral neuralgic symptoms indicate demyelination until proven otherwise.

problems.description: Persistent burning pain across one side of the face following a blistering skin rash, continuing long after the skin has healed.
problems.etiology: Varicella zoster — the same virus that caused chickenpox years ago — sits dormant in the dorsal root ganglion or trigeminal ganglion and reactivates as shingles [1]. The reason it reactivates is a drop in immune surveillance: you see it most in the immunocompromised, alcoholics, and the elderly [1]. Up to 15% of shingles episodes go on to leave behind post-herpetic neuralgia — a chronic neuropathic state that can persist for years [2].
problems.presentation: It starts with pre-eruption pain, then painful vesicles break out on skin or mucosa confined strictly to a nerve distribution — always unilateral, never crossing the midline [1]. Facial and oral lesions follow the trigeminal branches [1]. The vesicles typically clear in two to four weeks [2]. What happens is that in some patients the pain doesn't go with the rash — it persists as severe post-herpetic neuralgia that may continue for years [2].
problems.results: If you catch shingles within three days of the first vesicle, aggressive aciclovir treatment reduces both the chance of post-herpetic neuralgia developing and its severity in immunocompromised patients [2]. One important red flag: if the eye is involved, urgent ophthalmology referral is mandatory, as corneal ulceration and visual loss are real risks [2].
problems.definingCharacteristics: Separation from other neuropain entries rests on the sequence: a preceding vesicular rash in a trigeminal dermatome is required for this diagnosis [2]. The distribution is always unilateral, never crossing the midline [1].
problems.treatment: The goal is to interrupt the process early. Aciclovir within three days of the first vesicle — that's the window [2]. Symptomatic management is the mainstay otherwise [2].
problems.prognosis: Post-herpetic neuralgia may run for years [2]. Aciclovir within three days of the first vesicle reduces the incidence and severity of post-herpetic neuralgia in immunocompromised patients — so early treatment in the acute episode is the best chance to avoid this outcome [2].

citations.quote: Shingles is commoner in the immunocompromised, alcoholics, and elderly people. It is confined to the distribution of a nerve, the virus staying either in the dorsal root ganglion of a peripheral nerve or the trigeminal ganglion. It always presents as a unilateral lesion, never crossing the midline. Facial or oral lesions may arise in the area supplied by the branches of the trigeminal nerve.

∆: pre-eruption pain, followed by development of painful vesicles on skin or oral mucosa, which rupture to give ulcers or crusting skin wounds, in the distribution outlined previously. These usually clear in 2–4 weeks, with scarring and pigmentations and is often followed by severe post-herpetic neuralgia (up to 15%) which may continue for years. Rx: symptomatic relief for chickenpox. There is some evidence to suggest that aggressive early Rx of shingles with aciclovir (within 3 days of first vesicle) ↓ the incidence and severity of post-herpetic neuralgia in immunocompromised patients. Urgent referral to an ophthalmologist is required if the eye is involved as there is a risk of corneal ulceration and visual loss.

problems.description: Sudden onset of one-sided facial drooping, inability to close the eye or smile, often preceded by pain around the ear.
problems.etiology: Inflammation of cranial nerve VII as it travels through the stylomastoid canal [1]. What makes this useful clinically is the lower-versus-upper motor neurone distinction: the forehead gets bilateral cortical innervation, so upper motor neurone strokes spare it. If the forehead is involved, you're looking at lower motor neurone pathology [2]. Bell's palsy sits alongside Ramsay Hunt syndrome, Guillain-Barré, trauma, and malignant infiltration as causes of lower motor neurone facial palsy [3].
problems.presentation: Facial paralysis is the headline, but the thing is — pain around the ear, often radiating to the jaw, precedes or appears alongside the paralysis in about half of cases [1]. Test the nerve properly: ask the patient to raise their eyebrows, screw their eyes shut, whistle, smile, and show their teeth [2]. Taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue may also drop out, because the chorda tympani is caught up in the same nerve [2].
problems.results: The three-day window matters. Steroids started within 72 hours of onset give the best chance of full recovery [1]. Without treatment, 20% won't fully recover [1]. Aciclovir — alone or combined with steroids — doesn't improve outcomes over steroids alone, so don't lean on it as the main intervention [1]. The eye is the urgent priority: the patient can't blink, so the cornea needs protection now [1].
problems.definingCharacteristics: Bell's palsy is the only condition in this origin presenting primarily as a motor deficit rather than pain. The facial droop with inability to close the eye, whistle, or smile is pathognomonic — no other neuropain entry produces lower motor neurone facial paralysis [2][3]. The ear pain that often accompanies it can draw attention before the motor signs are obvious [1].
problems.treatment: Start steroids within three days of onset [1]. Protect the cornea with an eye pad immediately — eye closure is gone and the cornea is unprotected [1]. Aciclovir combined with steroids, or aciclovir alone, does not improve recovery over steroids alone, so steroids are the intervention [1].
problems.prognosis: Treat promptly and most patients recover fully. Without treatment, 20% will be left with residual deficit [1]. The takeaway: this is one condition where the treatment window is genuinely time-sensitive.

citations.quote: Caused by inflammation of cranial nerve VII in the stylomastoid canal. Although the main symptom is facial paralysis, pain in or around the ear, often radiating to the jaw, precedes or develops at the same time in ~50% of cases. Rx: steroids improve chance for full recovery if Rx early (within 3 days of onset). If no Rx, 20% of patients will not completely recover. Protect cornea with eye pad. Combining aciclovir with steroid or aciclovir alone does not appear to improve recovery over steroid alone.

The facial nerve is motor to the muscles of facial expression and stapedius, secretomotor to the submandibular and sublingual salivary glands, and relays taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue via the chorda tympani. It is tested by having the patient raise their eyebrows, screw their eyes shut, whistle, smile, and show their teeth. Upper and lower motor neurone lesions can be distinguished because the forehead has a degree of bilateral innervation and is relatively spared in upper motor neurone lesions.

Lower motor neurone paralysis can be caused by Bell's palsy, trauma, infiltration by malignant tumours, Ramsay Hunt syndrome, or Guillain–Barré syndrome (post-viral polyneuritis, may even appear to be bilateral).

problems.description: Constant deep aching or burning pain at a tooth or extraction site that persists or worsens despite technically sound dental treatment.
problems.etiology: Diagnosis of exclusion. It accounts for a surprisingly large proportion of facial pain presentations, and the demographic is striking: mostly middle-aged women, around 70% [1]. The reason it's so easily missed is that the symptoms don't map onto any nerve distribution or known pathological process — so clinicians keep hunting for an organic cause, and patients drift through multiple specialist disciplines without a diagnosis [1]. There may be a florid psychiatric history; 50% turn out to be depressed or hypochondriacal [1].
problems.presentation: Pain is deep, constant, aching or burning — no paroxysms, no touch trigger [1]. Classically there are no relieving or exacerbating factors at all [1]. The interesting bit: patients describe continuous, unbearable pain yet sleeping and eating are not obviously disturbed — that mismatch is a useful pointer [1]. Most analgesics are said not to help, though many patients haven't actually tried adequate analgesia [1].
problems.results: Several features point toward a psychogenic aetiology: pain that's imprecisely localised, crosses the midline, frequently migrates, or is described in bizarre or grossly exaggerated terms [1]. All investigations are essentially normal; no objective signs are demonstrable [1]. Once you've excluded organic causes, tricyclic antidepressants, gabapentin, or pregabalin can help, and a specialist pain team with psychological input is often the right destination [1].
problems.definingCharacteristics: The defining feature is pain that's unrelated to anatomical nerve distribution or any known pathological process, with no objective signs on examination and all investigations normal [1]. The demographic pointer — mostly middle-aged women — and the psychiatric co-morbidity (50% depressed or hypochondriacal) further characterise the group [1].
problems.treatment: First: exclude every possible organic cause. Then and only then: tricyclic antidepressants, gabapentin, or pregabalin [1]. Refer to the specialist pain team — psychological input genuinely improves outcomes [1].
problems.prognosis: Guarded. The condition is chronic and resistant to conventional analgesia [1]. Tricyclics and gabapentinoids can help in some patients [1]. Psychological input via the specialist pain team may be of benefit [1].

citations.quote: Diagnosis is of exclusion. Constitutes a large proportion of patients presenting with facial pain. Mostly middle aged women (70%). Classically, their symptoms are unrelated to anatomical distribution of nerves or any known pathological process, and these patients have often been through a number of specialist disciplines in an attempt to establish a ∆. This ∆ tends to be used as a catch-all for a large group of patients, with the connecting underlying supposition that the pain is of psychogenic origin. There may be a florid psychiatric history or undiagnosed depression (50% are depressed or hypochondriacal). Pointers to a psychogenic aetiology include imprecise localization, crosses midline, often bilateral pain, frequently moves to another site or 'all over the place'. Bizarre or grossly exaggerated descriptions of pain. Pain is described as deep, constant ache or burning and there are no relieving or exacerbating factors. Sleeping and eating are not obviously disturbed, despite continuous unbearable pain. Most analgesics are said to be unhelpful, although many will not have tried adequate analgesia. No objective signs are demonstrable and all investigations are essentially normal. After exclusion of any possible organic cause, tricyclic antidepressants, gabapentin, or pregabalin can help. The specialist pain team with access to psychological input may be of help.

problems.description: Severe boring pain around one eye, lasting 30–60 minutes, recurring nightly in clusters — with a watering eye and blocked nostril on the same side.
problems.etiology: Similar aetiology to migraine, but a completely different clinical picture [1]. Most sufferers describe alcohol intolerance — alcohol reliably triggers an attack during a cluster period [1].
problems.presentation: Periodic attacks of severe, unilateral pain — boring or burning, located around the eye, lasting 30–60 minutes [1]. What happens alongside the pain is the key: the eye on the affected side waters, the conjunctiva becomes congested, and there's nasal discharge — all ipsilateral autonomic features [1]. Attacks follow a clock-like pattern, often hitting at the same time of night ('alarm clock wakening'), and cluster densely over weeks before a longer remission interval [1]. Alcohol intolerance is almost universal during active periods [1].
problems.results: The interesting bit diagnostically: oxygen inhalation in an acute attack is both effective and diagnostic [1]. If O2 relieves it, you've confirmed the diagnosis. NSAIDs, ergotamine or sumatriptan, and intranasal lidocaine are also used acutely [1].
problems.definingCharacteristics: Three features simultaneously are pathognomonic and absent in every other entry in this origin: (1) strict nocturnal periodicity with an 'alarm clock' pattern, (2) autonomic symptoms ipsilateral to the pain (lacrimation, conjunctival injection, nasal congestion), and (3) clustering periods with remission intervals [1].
problems.treatment: Acute attack: O2 inhalation first — it's effective and confirms the diagnosis [1]. Also use NSAIDs, ergotamine or sumatriptan, or intranasal lidocaine [1]. Prophylaxis: pizotifen [1].
problems.prognosis: Attacks tend to cluster densely over a period of time, followed by a longer period of remission [1].

citations.quote: This has a similar aetiology to migraine but with a different clinical presentation: periodic attacks of severe, unilateral pain, boring or burning in character, lasting 30–60min, located around the eye; commonly associated with autonomic symptoms such as watering of eye on affected side, congestion of conjunctiva, and nasal discharge. Attacks often occur at a particular time of night (early morning 'alarm clock wakening'), and tend to be closely concentrated over a period of time, followed by a longer period of remission. Most sufferers describe alcohol intolerance. Rx: O2 inhalation (effectiveness in acute attack is diagnostic), NSAIDs, ergotamine or sumatriptan, intranasal lidocaine. Pizotifen is used prophylactically.

problems.description: Numbness, tingling, or altered sensation of the lip, chin, or tongue following surgical removal of a lower wisdom tooth.
problems.conditionName: Inferior alveolar, lingual, or mental nerve injury following lower third molar extraction
problems.etiology:
Three nerves are at risk during lower third molar surgery: the inferior alveolar nerve, the mental nerve, and the lingual nerve [1]. Radiographic red flags you need to know [2]:

- Proximity to the nerve canal
- Narrowing or diversion of the canal
- Darkening of root or interruption of the white canal lines
- Interruption of the lamina dura
- Juxta-apical area

Reported rates for conventional surgical removal are 8% temporary and 3.6% permanent altered sensation [3].
problems.presentation: Paraesthesia or anaesthesia appears in the distribution of the IAN (lower lip and chin) or lingual nerve (anterior tongue, floor of mouth) [1][5]. There's also a separate variant worth knowing: mental nerve compression by a denture flange after alveolar resorption, which produces an electric-shock sensation with a background ache that builds through the day and eases overnight [4].
problems.results: Reported rates for conventional surgical removal are 8% temporary and 3.6% permanent altered sensation [3]. Coronectomy was developed specifically to reduce this risk when radiographic signs show roots closely involved with the ID canal: remove the crown, leave the roots, and the nerve never gets close to the operative field [3].
problems.definingCharacteristics: The discriminating feature within this origin is the surgical trigger: altered sensation follows a specific operative event (third molar extraction or other lower jaw surgery), and is in the distribution of the IAN or lingual nerve [1][5]. The patient is warned of this risk prior to surgery [5].
problems.treatment: Before surgery: consent the patient about the possibility of IAN and lingual nerve damage [5]. If radiographic signs show roots closely involved with the ID canal, consider coronectomy — intentional crown removal with root retention — rather than complete extraction [3]. One firm rule on operative technique: approach bone and tooth removal from the buccal side — lingual manipulation causes unnecessary lingual nerve morbidity [6].
problems.prognosis: Temporary altered sensation: 8%. Permanent: 3.6% for conventional surgical removal [3]. Coronectomy compares favourably in terms of nerve outcomes [3].

citations.quote: It is crucial that key anatomical structures are identified by the surgeon prior to and during implant placement to ensure injuries (e.g. laceration, section, or compression) are avoided where possible. Moderate- to high-risk structures include the inferior alveolar nerve, mental nerve, lingual nerve, and sublingual/submental arteries.

Radiographic signs of ↑ risk of nerve damage include: Proximity to nerve canal. Narrowing or diversion of canal. Darkening of root/interrupting white lines of canal. Interruption of lamina dura. Juxta-apical area.

Coronectomy compares favourably to surgical removal of lower wisdom teeth in terms of altered sensation: reported rates for conventional surgical removal are 8% temporary, and 3.6% permanent (personal rates vary). There is a similar incidence of dry socket (10–12%).

Mental nerve compression by a denture flange following alveolar resorption is a common problem, producing a sensation like an electric shock but with a background ache which ↑ during the day and ↓ overnight.
Warn the patient about pain, trismus, swelling, and the possibility of damage to the ID and lingual nerves.
There is now good evidence to suggest that manipulation from the lingual aspect results in unnecessary lingual nerve morbidity. Bone and tooth removal should be from a buccal approach.
